title: Playing trumpet behind blues singers
summary: Punch explains filling in when the singer cuts out and notes Johnny Dunn's plunger.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Bessie, Mamie, Ma Rainey: the classic blues queens

blocks.x: Now what about in playing trumpet behind the singers? How did that develop?

Well, we used to do it. When the singer, singer, say and listen and cut out, we fill in. But now they go right along with the singer, you know what I mean? Like somebody say, I've got the blues and the blues about to kill me. I've got the blues and the blues about to kill me. And if I lose the blues, I won't be. You know what I mean? That's what we used to play. When the singer cut out, we come in. When she come back, we cut out. Drop under, you know. But now they go right along with the singer. Who would sing the blues then? Oh man, we had plenty of blues singers then. I mean, you know, like Bessie Smith and Manly Smith and all of them. When we got the sky out in front of them, everybody playing behind the singers, you know. Of course, there was that boy Johnny Dunn and he used that plunger like he was talking about. That's the first man who made me lack a plunger, him. A girl named Edith Wilson sung a song about Mammy. Mammy, when she got to the end, she said, Mammy, when I get back home, he said, guagga guagga guagga. Boy, you're talking about something I like. That's the only thing I like about the whole song. He put it in there. Guagga guagga guagga guagga. He made that pretty.
